structure.title: Enslavement and learning
structure.text: Early chapters reconstruct family separation, plantation violence, and the struggle to acquire literacy.

structure.title: Resistance and testimony
structure.text: Later chapters follow changing forms of resistance and the narrator's emergence as a public witness. The appendix clarifies his religious criticism.

people.name: Douglass
people.text: Born enslaved in Maryland, Douglass tells his own life, from separation from his mother as an infant to his determination to be free.

people.name: Literacy
people.text: Learning to read, against his enslavers' wishes, shows Douglass both how slavery works and that he does not have to accept it.

people.name: Slaveholding authority
people.text: The book shows slavery kept in place not only by the whip but by keeping enslaved people ignorant, divided and unsure even of their own birthdays.

context.title: A public testimony
context.text: The narrative addresses readers in a society where slavery is defended and its victims' credibility contested. Precision is part of its intervention.
context.takeaway: Attend to how evidence is established.

context.title: Christianity and hypocrisy
context.text: Douglass distinguishes religious profession from the practices of slaveholders. The appendix prevents criticism of one from being carelessly conflated with the other.

notice.text: Notice restrictions on names, dates, and learning.
notice.why: Deprivation of knowledge is part of domination.

notice.text: Follow changes in the narrator's ability to act.
notice.why: Freedom emerges through difficult, specific efforts.

opening: Frederick Douglass hears a slaveholder explain why teaching him to read would make him unfit for slavery. The warning gives him a purpose. Learning opens a world his enslavers need to keep closed, while making his own captivity more painful to understand. Douglass writes about violence, calculated ignorance, and the struggle to recover authority over his body and mind with a precision that refuses the reader comfortable distance. The man whom slavery was supposed to render voiceless becomes an exacting witness against it.
